questions.stem: The initial rate of a reaction is measured

options.text: At the very start of the reaction, at t = 0
options.explanation: Initial means before any significant concentration change.
Midpoint times give average, not initial, rates.
No rate information survives completion.

options.text: At the steepest point of the curve only
options.explanation: The steepest point may occur later; initial means t = 0.

questions.stem: The tangent method for finding an initial rate involves

options.explanation: No such quotient exists.

options.text: Drawing a tangent to the concentration-time curve at t = 0 and computing its gradient
options.explanation: The starting gradient is the initial rate.
Endpoints carry no rate information.
That describes the clock method.

questions.stem: In the calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid demonstration, tangents are added because

options.text: The gas volume is too small to read
options.explanation: Volume readability is not the reason.
Drawing tangents changes nothing physically.

options.text: Each acid concentration gives its own curve, and each starting gradient is that run's initial rate
options.explanation: One tangent per curve reads one initial rate.

options.text: The curves are all straight lines
options.explanation: Curved or straight, tangents give the starting rate.

questions.stem: A clock reaction measures the time t for a visual change, and the initial rate is taken as

options.explanation: That would make slower reactions have larger rates.
No square relationship applies.
The timing is the whole measurement.
Faster changes mean shorter times, so inverse proportionality.

questions.stem: The key assumption behind clock reactions is that

options.text: The rate stays roughly constant between mixing and the moment the clock change is seen
options.explanation: The 1/t conversion presumes a steady early rate.

options.text: The rate rises steeply throughout the run
options.explanation: That would break the method.

options.text: The visual change happens by itself
options.explanation: The change marks a fixed extent of reaction.
Temperature is held constant.

questions.stem: State how a tangent yields an initial rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw the tangent at t = 0 on the concentration-time graph and calculate its gradient; that gradient is the initial rate.

questions.stem: State what a clock reaction times and how the initial rate is taken from it.
questions.modelAnswer: It times the moment of a single visual change, and the initial rate is taken as proportional to 1/t.

questions.stem: Explain why the tangent at t = 0 gives the cleanest reading of the rate equation.
questions.modelAnswer: At the start, concentrations equal the values the experimenter chose, so the measured gradient corresponds to known concentrations without any drift; later points mix changing concentrations into the reading.

questions.stem: A clock reaction records 25 s for the colour change at one concentration and 50 s at half that concentration. What does the comparison suggest about the order?
questions.modelAnswer: Halving the concentration doubles the time, so 1/t halves, meaning the rate halved with the concentration - behaviour consistent with first order.

questions.stem: The initial rate proportional to 1/t for a measured time of 40 s is

options.explanation: That is 1/0.04, mixing units.
That is t, not 1/t.
A decimal slip of the true quotient.

questions.stem: The specimen clock table shows the rate doubling when concentration doubles, which identifies the reaction as

options.explanation: Second order would quadruple the rate.
Third order would give an eightfold rise.

options.text: First order with respect to that reactant
options.explanation: Doubling on doubling is the proportionality signature.
Zero order would show no rate change.

questions.stem: Clock-reaction initial rates become less accurate when the measured time is long because

options.explanation: Timing devices are not the issue.
The endpoint is fixed, not strengthened.
The quotient is always defined for positive t.

options.text: The constant-rate assumption weakens as reactants deplete during the long wait
options.explanation: Drifting concentrations break the 1/t shortcut.

questions.stem: In the clock table, 1/t values across different concentrations can be compared directly because

options.text: Each 1/t carries the same proportionality to its run's initial rate
options.explanation: The same milestone and assumption apply to every run.

options.text: The units of 1/t change with concentration
options.explanation: Units stay s^-1 throughout.

options.text: Each run used a different indicator
options.explanation: One indicator system is used throughout.
Runs are held at fixed temperature.

questions.stem: A clock run records a much longer time than the others in its set. The best inference is

options.explanation: Higher concentration shortens the time.

options.text: Its initial rate is the smallest and the least accurate of the set
options.explanation: Long times mean slow early rates and weakening assumptions.

options.text: Its initial rate is the largest
options.explanation: Large rates give short times.
The endpoint was still reached.

questions.stem: State the 1/t conversion for a measured time of 40 s.
questions.modelAnswer: 1/40 = 0.025 s^-1, the quantity proportional to the initial rate.

questions.stem: State the accuracy trend of clock-reaction rates as measured times lengthen.
questions.modelAnswer: Accuracy falls: short times give initial rates close to the true value, long times drift from it.

questions.stem: Explain why 1/t can serve as a stand-in for the initial rate in clock experiments.
questions.modelAnswer: Every run triggers the same small extent of reaction before the clock change appears, so the distance travelled is fixed and speed equals that fixed extent divided by time, making rate proportional to 1/t.

questions.stem: Two clock runs give times of 20 s and 40 s. State the ratio of their initial rates.
questions.modelAnswer: The rates are proportional to 1/20 and 1/40, so the faster run's initial rate is twice the slower run's.
